reason: While the text does depict a national conflict between the Hebrew people (בְנֵֽי־ יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל) and the Egyptians (מִצְרַ֖יִם), the entire narrative is fundamentally framed as religious. God appears to Moses in the burning bush, identifies Himself as 'the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,' and frames the liberation as rooted in divine covenant and personal intervention ('I will be with you'). The oppression is understood within a religious theological context—God's concern for His covenant people—rather than as a purely national political conflict. The statement's claim that the conflict is 'not...religious' contradicts the explicitly theological framework of this passage.
